segments.narration: Workers were told to lick brushes loaded with radium. New Jersey, nineteen seventeen, painting glow-in-the-dark watch dials.
The job was well paid and the paint was fun. Some of the women painted their nails and teeth with it for a night out.
Radium behaves like calcium in the body. It went into their bones and stayed, and their jaws began to break apart.
The company said their illnesses were syphilis. Its own consultants had already documented the danger.
Five women sued in nineteen twenty-seven and settled. Their cases forced the law to recognise disease caused by work, and shaped US safety standards.

verdicts.claim: Dial painters in the 1910s and 1920s were instructed to point their radium-loaded brushes with their lips
verdicts.note: Lip-pointing was standard practice taught to dial painters.

verdicts.claim: Some dial painters applied the luminous paint to their nails and teeth for amusement
verdicts.note: 78% of the claim's wording appears in the reference article

verdicts.claim: Ingested radium deposits in bone, causing necrosis of the jaw and bone tumours in the dial painters
verdicts.note: Radium's chemical similarity to calcium drove bone deposition and radium jaw.

verdicts.claim: The employer publicly attributed the workers' illnesses to other causes despite internal knowledge of radium's hazards
verdicts.note: US Radium disputed the diagnoses while internal studies indicated harm.

verdicts.claim: Litigation by the dial painters helped establish employers' liability for occupational disease in the United States
verdicts.note: 67% of the claim's wording appears in the reference article
